analysis.one_liner: Ends the tax break that lets US corporations put off paying US tax on foreign profits and closes related loopholes.
analysis.headline: The bill never left the House Ways and Means Committee and never received a vote before Congress ended on January 3, 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: US corporations generally pay no US tax on profits their foreign subsidiaries earn until the money is brought home, which encourages companies to park profits overseas and book income in low-tax countries. This bill would tax foreign profits as they are earned, tax previously untaxed offshore stockpiles (with up to eight years to pay), strip large oil companies of a foreign tax credit, tax foreign companies actually run from the United States, limit interest deductions for foreign-owned US subsidiaries, and stop companies from dodging US tax by relocating on paper to a lower-tax country. It was referred to the tax-writing committee and died there.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary taxpayers, because multinational corporations currently shifting profits offshore would pay more US tax, broadening the base and potentially reducing pressure to tax other income more heavily. Treasury would also collect tax on the roughly $2.6 trillion in offshore profits American companies had accumulated by that era, paid in installments over up to eight years. Honest domestic competitors that pay full US tax would face fairer competition against companies that minimize tax through foreign booking.

how_it_helps.text: The bill eliminates deferral: starting in 2018, the foreign-source income of controlled foreign corporations counts as subpart F income taxed currently to US shareholders, ending the incentive to park profits offshore indefinitely.
It requires US shareholders to include accumulated previously deferred foreign income as taxable income, with an election to pay the liability in up to eight equal installments.

It denies the foreign tax credit to large integrated oil companies (over $1 billion in gross receipts and at least 500,000 barrels of daily worldwide crude production) that are 'dual capacity taxpayers' — companies that pay foreign levies that function partly as payments for access to resources rather than true income taxes.
It restores the per-country limitation on the foreign tax credit and limits the credit to income actually subject to US tax.

It treats foreign corporations that are publicly traded or hold $50 million or more in assets, and that are managed and controlled primarily in the United States, as domestic corporations for income tax purposes.

It limits interest deductions for US subsidiaries of foreign-owned financial reporting groups with excess domestic indebtedness, a rule aimed at earnings-stripping — the practice of loading US subsidiaries with debt to related foreign affiliates to erase US taxable income.

It expands the definition of inverted corporations so that any post-May 2014 deal in which former US owners keep more than 50% of the new foreign parent is treated as a US company for tax purposes, regardless of the prior 60%/80% ownership thresholds in current law.

analysis.who_pays: Shareholders of multinational corporations holding untaxed offshore profits, large integrated oil companies that benefit from the foreign tax credit, US subsidiaries of foreign parents using interest deductions to strip earnings, foreign companies managed from the United States, and companies that have inverted or plan to invert. Corporate income taxes are ultimately borne in part by shareholders and, to a lesser extent, by workers through wages and consumers through prices.
analysis.who_pays_short: Multinational shareholders and large oil companies

drawbacks.text: Ending deferral without also lowering the US corporate rate would tax active foreign earnings at the full US rate on top of foreign taxes, arguably making US-headquartered companies less competitive against foreign rivals and encouraging real relocation of headquarters and operations abroad rather than just paper profits.

Denying the foreign tax credit to large oil companies' dual-capacity payments would, in some countries, result in the same income being taxed twice — once by the host government and once by the United States — a cost that could fall on the companies' operations and employees rather than only shareholders.

A one-time tax on accumulated offshore earnings, even spread over eight installments, is a large liquidity hit to companies, and the bill offers no reduced rate for repatriating those historic earnings, unlike later proposals that paired inclusion with a lower rate.
Retroactive-style rules for inversions completed since May 2014 would reach deals already done, which businesses argue violates expectations set under prior law.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core of the bill — ending deferral and taxing existing offshore stockpiles — would meaningfully reduce the gap between what profitable multinationals owe and pay, and the oil-company credit fix targets a well-documented loophole. But the bill was designed as pure loophole-closing with no rate relief or repatriation discount, which makes its competitive costs real and explains why few members signed on; a more durable version of this debate would need to pair base-protection with rate changes. On balance it would have shifted tax burden toward large corporations and away from other taxpayers, at some cost to the competitiveness of US-headquartered firms.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced and sat there with no hearing, markup, or floor vote through the end of the 115th Congress.

narrative.text: Rep. Janice Schakowsky introduced the bill on March 9, 2017, with a single Democratic cosponsor.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means on the day of introduction.
The action history shows no further action — no hearing, no markup, no committee or floor vote — before the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Multinational corporations with untaxed offshore profits and large oil companies using the foreign tax credit came out ahead, because the bill died in committee and their tax treatment was left unchanged for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral — no hearing, markup, or vote is recorded in the action history.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken; the bill's two sponsors were both Democrats, so its reception in the Republican-controlled committee and chamber cannot be measured from the record.

industries.note: The bill would end their ability to defer US tax on foreign profits and would tax previously deferred offshore earnings. Their continued deferral was a major reason US corporations reported large profits in low-tax jurisdictions while paying little US tax on them.

Companies over $1 billion in receipts producing at least 500,000 barrels a day would lose the foreign tax credit on payments to countries that do not levy a general income tax — payments that often function as resource-access fees. This subsidy channel would close.

Post-2014 deals keeping former US owners above 50% ownership would be taxed as domestic corporations, sharply narrowing the tax benefit of reincorporating abroad. Tax advisory and deal practices built around inversions would lose a product line.

Firms that design offshore profit-shifting, earnings-stripping, and inversion structures would lose the demand this bill targets. Curbing these practices would simplify compliance for ordinary domestic firms that cannot afford such planning.

industries.industry: US subsidiaries of foreign parent groups
industries.note: The bill would cap interest deductions for members of foreign-parented financial reporting groups with excess domestic debt, targeting earnings-stripping that erodes the US tax base.
